opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the parts I find most exciting about the recurrent-depth setup. Because the model is trained to iterate a shared block in latent space a variable number of times, you get adaptive compute almost for free at inference time. You don't have to train a separate router or a mixture-of-depths mechanism; you can just watch the latent state and stop once it stops changing meaningfully.

What we did is fairly simple: for each token, we look at something like the KL divergence between the output distributions of successive iterations, and once that drops below a threshold, we exit for that token. Easy tokens, like finishing a common word or producing punctuation, converge in a handful of steps. Harder tokens, say in a math problem or where the model actually has to make a decision, keep iterating much longer. Seeing that emerge without explicitly training for it was really nice, because it suggests the model is spending its compute where it matters.

There are some practical wrinkles. If tokens exit at different depths, later tokens may need key-value cache entries from recurrence steps that earlier tokens never computed. It turned out you can be pretty relaxed about that: reusing the most recent available state, or sharing the cache across iterations, works surprisingly well, which also saves memory.

More broadly, I think of per-token early exit as one piece of a bigger picture where compute at test time becomes a dial rather than a fixed property of the architecture. You can use it for efficiency, but you can also go the other way and let the model think longer on the tokens that are genuinely hard, all in continuous latent space instead of verbalizing every step as chain-of-thought. And because the recurrence makes the model behave a bit like a diffusion or fixed-point process, it also opens the door to things like self-speculative decoding, where fewer iterations draft and more iterations verify. So there's a lot of room to explore there.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I'm actually most excited about with this architecture, because it falls out of the design almost for free. The model is built around a recurrent block that you can iterate as many times as you want, and during training we sample the number of iterations randomly, so the model never gets to rely on a fixed depth. What that means at inference time is that the model isn't committed to any particular budget per token. You can run the recurrence for, say, four steps on one token and sixty-four on the next, and the model is fine with that.

And the nice thing is you can actually measure convergence. Because it's a recurrence operating on a latent state, you can look at how much the state changes from one iteration to the next. For a lot of tokens, it settles very quickly, the difference drops below some threshold after just a handful of steps, and continuing to iterate doesn't change the output distribution in any meaningful way. For other tokens, the harder ones, it keeps moving for much longer. So you get this very natural per-token exit criterion that you didn't have to train a separate halting head for, which is something people in the adaptive compute space have struggled with for a long time, going back to ACT and PonderNet and so on.

What we found looking at this is that the "difficulty" the model expresses this way is fairly intuitive. Function words, things that are highly predictable from context, converge almost immediately. Tokens where the model is actually doing something, where it's in the middle of an arithmetic chain, or resolving an ambiguous reference, or at a point in a math problem where it has to decide what to do next, those take much longer. So the computation really is being allocated toward the places where it matters, and you're not paying the full cost on every token the way you would with a fixed-depth transformer.

I should be honest about the caveats, though. Exiting early on individual tokens interacts awkwardly with batching, because if one sequence in your batch wants to keep going and another is done, you have to handle that somehow, and the engineering there is not trivial. You also have to be careful about the KV cache, because tokens that exited at different depths have been through different amounts of computation, and you need the downstream tokens to be able to attend to them consistently. We've done some of that work, but I'd say the systems side is less mature than the modeling side. And there's a question of whether the convergence criterion is the right proxy for "the model has figured it out," or whether there are cases where the state looks stable but the model would actually benefit from more steps. I think it mostly works, but I wouldn't claim it's perfectly calibrated.

Longer term, I think the direction this points to is one where test-time compute becomes a knob that's much more fine-grained than what we currently do with chain of thought. Right now, if you want a model to think harder, you make it generate more tokens, which is coarse and also forces the model to verbalize everything through the bottleneck of language. With latent recurrence you can spend compute without emitting tokens, and you can spend it unevenly across the sequence. Combining those two things, deciding per token how much to think, and doing that thinking in a continuous space rather than discrete tokens, is what I find really compelling about the approach.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s one of the most exciting possibilities, because you don’t necessarily want to spend the same amount of computation on every token. Some tokens are fairly predictable, and others might require quite a bit more reasoning. With a model that iterates in latent space, you can potentially vary how many iterations you run before producing each token.

The tricky part is deciding when to stop. You could look at whether the latent state has stabilized, or whether the prediction is changing as you do more iterations. But being stable or confident doesn’t necessarily mean you’re correct. And a token that looks easy to predict might still be a useful place to do computation that helps with what comes afterward.

So I see early exiting as a very natural direction, but the stopping criterion is an important research question. Ideally, the model would learn to allocate computation where it actually improves the answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s one of the exciting possibilities. If you’re iterating in latent space, you don’t necessarily have to spend the same amount of computation on every token. Some tokens might need very little processing, while others could benefit from several more iterations.

The tricky part is deciding when to stop. You need a signal that says additional computation is unlikely to help, and you need to learn that without the model simply choosing to exit immediately. There’s also a practical issue: if every token takes a different number of steps, it becomes harder to batch that computation efficiently on a GPU.

So I see a lot of potential there, but I’d distinguish the ability to vary computation from having a reliable, efficient policy for doing it. That second part is really the interesting research question.
